title: Improvement ain’t a bad word
author: Jo Castelino
summary: Jo Castelino uses the case of an experienced teacher, Mr T, who sits through retrieval-practice CPD believing he already does it, to examine why many teachers find professional development and performance management patronising. She argues that the fix is to value staff expertise, explain the rationale behind a strategy, and use examples and non-examples so a strategy does not mutate into something harmless but useless, such as students copying answers from their books. Performance management should name a specific aspect of practice to develop, not hand out a blanket goal. The piece fits Practice & Culture because its subject is the profession side of teaching: CPD, improvement culture and how teachers experience being developed.
points: Confident, experienced teachers often hear nothing new in CPD and read the call to improve as an insult.
Explaining the rationale for a strategy and inviting experts on staff to share their experience makes implementation genuinely school-wide.
Examples and non-examples reveal when a strategy has mutated, as when students look back in their books and copy rather than retrieve.
Performance management should target a specific aspect of practice rather than a one-size-fits-all goal such as retrieval Do Nows.
Improvement is about getting better, and CPD should respect staff expertise rather than patronise it.
quotes: Mr T definitely does ‘retrieval’- he just doesn’t call it that. He asks questions on previous topics quite regularly. But he doesn’t always ask them at the start of the lesson.

I think it is also helpful to explain the rationale behind anything that is being implemented. Is it to acheive consistency so that retrieval is a major part of all lessons? Can this work in all subjects?

If some staff are already incorporating this strategy into their practice, could they share their experience of it in CPD sessions? Staff that are already experts in the strategy will feel valued and other staff can see that the strategy is worth incorporating.
I think when leading CPD, discussions around examples and non-examples of a strategy can be powerful. I know that I would have benefitted from this when I first heard about retrieval.

When it comes to performance management, we need to discuss what aspect of a teacher’s practice could benefit from development instead of providing a blanket, one-size-fits-all goal. Instead of telling teachers to include retrieval in their Do Nows, have discussions about what that retrieval looks like, when it is appropriate to incorporate it, and how it is actually implemented.

We must be open to making our practice efficient, collaborating and sharing our experiences with teachers so that each and every one of us can have a positive impact on our students. And this should happen with CPD that is not patronising but includes and values the expertise of staff.
